title: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall
lead: A helicopter crash in Peru killed four Americans working on a pipeline. Their survivors sued the Colombian helicopter company in Texas, relying on its Houston negotiations and years of purchases and training in Fort Worth.

actors.name: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. (Helicol)
actors.role: Bogotá-based helicopter company and defendant contesting Texas jurisdiction.

actors.name: Consorcio
actors.role: Peruvian pipeline consortium that employed the decedents and hired Helicol.

actors.name: The survivors and representatives
actors.role: Wrongful-death plaintiffs, none domiciled in Texas.

proceedings: Texas trial proceedings produced a wrongful-death judgment against Helicol. The intermediate appellate court reversed for lack of jurisdiction; the Texas Supreme Court ultimately sustained jurisdiction on rehearing. The U.S. Supreme Court reversed on the general-jurisdiction question presented.
limits: The majority treated the claims as unrelated to Texas contacts; Brennan disputed that understanding. Specific-jurisdiction relationship questions were expressly reserved. This 1984 decision did not decide the merits of wrongful-death liability or certify present-day general-jurisdiction doctrine.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A Peruvian project requires helicopter transportation
sections.cue: How did a Colombian company become connected with Houston?
paragraphs: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A., known as Helicol, was based in Bogotá and transported personnel and supplies for oil and construction businesses in South America. Consorcio, a Peruvian consortium and alter ego of a joint venture headquartered in Houston, had contracted to build a pipeline for Peru’s state-owned oil company. It needed helicopters to move people, equipment, and materials.

At the venture’s request, Helicol’s chief executive traveled to Houston in 1974 to discuss price, availability, and operating arrangements. Helicol began work before the parties formally signed their Spanish-language agreement in Peru. The contract designated Lima as their residence, selected Peruvian courts for contractual disputes, and directed payments to Helicol’s New York bank account. Consorcio ultimately paid more than $5 million through checks drawn on a Houston bank, though Helicol received the money outside Texas.

sections.title: The company’s fleet also links it to Texas
sections.cue: What did the repeated purchasing relationship involve?
paragraphs: From 1970 through 1977, Helicol bought helicopters, parts, and accessories worth more than $4 million from Bell Helicopter Company in Fort Worth. Those helicopters comprised approximately eighty percent of its fleet. Helicol sent pilots to Texas for training and to ferry aircraft back to South America; management and maintenance personnel also visited for familiarization and technical consultation.

Those contacts did not include a Texas operating base. Helicol had no Texas office, establishment, resident employees, property, records, shareholders, or designated service agent. It was not licensed there, conducted no Texas helicopter operations, and sold no product reaching Texas. It neither recruited employees nor solicited business there and signed no contracts there.

sections.title: A fatal crash leads to a Texas judgment
sections.cue: What happened in the state courts?
paragraphs: On January 26, 1976, one of Helicol’s helicopters crashed in Peru, killing four United States citizens employed on the pipeline project. Their survivors and representatives brought wrongful-death actions in Texas against Helicol, Consorcio, and Bell. Neither the people killed nor the plaintiffs were domiciled in Texas.

Helicol specially appeared to contest personal jurisdiction and sought dismissal. The trial court rejected that objection. After a consolidated jury trial, it entered a $1,141,200 judgment for the plaintiffs against Helicol. The other defendants received directed verdicts on the plaintiffs’ claims, while Consorcio obtained a separate $70,000 cross-claim judgment against Helicol.

The Texas intermediate appellate court reversed for lack of jurisdiction. The Texas Supreme Court initially agreed, but withdrew its opinions on rehearing and ultimately sustained jurisdiction over three dissents. That court read the state long-arm statute to extend to the constitutional limit, leaving the U.S. Supreme Court to consider due process.

sections.title: The majority takes up jurisdiction over an unrelated claim
sections.cue: Why did the Court frame this as a general-jurisdiction case?
paragraphs: Justice Blackmun wrote for eight Justices. The majority understood the parties to have conceded that the wrongful-death claims neither arose out of nor related to Helicol’s Texas activities. It therefore considered general jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. Justice Brennan disputed that characterization of the plaintiffs’ position.

The majority compared Helicol with the company in Perkins, where the president of a displaced Philippine corporation directed its limited wartime business from Ohio. Helicol had no comparable concentrated corporate operation in Texas. One Houston negotiating visit did not constitute continuous and systematic activity of that kind.

Payments drawn on a Houston bank added little. Helicol had neither requested that bank nor negotiated its use; the payor ordinarily selected where to bank. Another party’s unilateral choice did not establish Helicol’s own forum relationship. The Court acknowledged that a payee might have a different role in unusual circumstances, such as concern about a bank’s financial health, but found none here.

sections.title: Purchases and related training do not supply the missing general jurisdiction
sections.cue: How narrowly did the Court state its purchasing rule?
paragraphs: The purchases and training were recurring contacts, but the majority relied on Rosenberg Bros. & Co. v. Curtis Brown Co., an earlier decision holding purchases and associated trips insufficient for jurisdiction over unrelated claims. International Shoe, the later minimum-contacts decision, had acknowledged Rosenberg. Training personnel to use purchased equipment remained part of the goods-and-services package; it did not create the broader corporate presence at issue.

The majority expressly limited that analysis to general jurisdiction. It left open Rosenberg’s continuing force when a claim arose out of or related to the purchases. It also reserved whether arising out of and related to described different connections and what relationship either required.

The plaintiffs proposed jurisdiction by necessity because they wanted a single forum for the defendants. They had not established that Colombia or Peru could not provide one. The Court declined to make a far-reaching jurisdictional change on that incomplete record.

sections.title: Brennan sees purposeful contacts and a relationship to this crash
sections.cue: Why would the dissent have sustained Texas jurisdiction?
paragraphs: Justice Brennan considered the aggregate of repeated purchases, training, technical consultations, and Houston negotiations sufficient purposeful commercial engagement to make Texas jurisdiction fair. He objected to relying on Rosenberg’s older corporate-presence reasoning without examining its fit with modern commerce and International Shoe. Perkins supplied an example, not a mandatory minimum.

Brennan separately found specific jurisdiction. The Houston negotiations produced the transportation arrangement used for the pipeline; the crashed helicopter was purchased in Texas; and the allegedly negligent pilot had trained there. The jury found negligent flying and lack of proper control to be proximate causes of the crash. For Brennan, the claim’s failure formally to arise from negligent Texas training did not make the Texas activities unrelated to it.

He distinguished a claim formally arising from an activity from one significantly related to it. Requiring only the former could make constitutional jurisdiction turn on state tort elements or complaint drafting. He would have upheld jurisdiction despite the accident’s Peruvian location. The majority reserved those relationship questions rather than adopting a holding rejecting his proposed standard.

sections.title: Reversal removes the jurisdictional foundation
sections.cue: What did the Supreme Court decide about the Texas judgment?
paragraphs: On April 24, 1984, the Supreme Court reversed the Texas Supreme Court, 8–1. Helicol’s contacts did not support the general jurisdiction on which the majority understood the case to rest. The decision removed the jurisdictional foundation for the Texas judgment under review; it did not find that the pilot exercised due care or decide a defense to the underlying wrongful-death liability.
